title: Downs and distance
summary: Four tries to go 10 yards, and what happens on fourth down.

steps.text: A down is one play. The offense gets 4 downs, four tries, to move the ball 10 yards. When you hear 1st and 10, that means first down with 10 yards to go.
Say the running back gains 4 yards on first down. Now it is 2nd and 6: second down, 6 yards still to go. Gain 6 or more and you earn a brand new first down, and a fresh set of four tries.

If the offense reaches 4th down and still has not gained the 10 yards, it has a choice. Go for it and risk giving the ball away right there. Punt the ball far down the field to the other team. Or, if close enough, kick a field goal for 3 points.

If the offense goes for it on 4th down and does not make it, the other team gets the ball right at that spot. That is called a turnover on downs. That is why most teams punt from their own side of the field.
Keep this in your head every play: what down is it, and how many yards to go? That one question explains almost every decision a coach makes.

quiz.prompt: How many downs does the offense get to gain 10 yards?
quiz.explanation: Four downs. Gain 10 yards within them and you get four more.

quiz.prompt: It is 1st and 10. The offense gains 3 yards. What is it now?
quiz.explanation: One down used, 3 of the 10 yards gained, so 7 yards still to go: 2nd and 7.

quiz.prompt: It is 3rd and 2. The offense gains 5 yards. What happens?
quiz.explanation: They needed 2 yards and got 5, so they earned a new first down: 1st and 10 again.

quiz.prompt: The offense is on its own 20-yard line on 4th and 8. What do most teams do?
quiz.explanation: Deep in your own end, a failed 4th down hands the other team the ball close to your goal. Punting pushes them far away.

quiz.prompt: What is a turnover on downs?
choices: Failing to gain the yards on 4th down, so the other team gets the ball there
quiz.explanation: Use all four downs without getting 10 yards and the ball goes to the other team at that spot.
